title: The First-Derivative (Sign) Test
quickIdea: Walk through the critical point and watch the sign of f': plus to minus is a maximum, minus to plus is a minimum, no change is neither.
remember: If f' changes from positive to negative at c, f has a local maximum at c.
If f' changes from negative to positive at c, f has a local minimum at c.
If f' keeps the same sign on both sides of c, there is no extremum at c, even if f'(c) = 0.
The test needs f continuous at c and f' of one sign on each side; it works at non-differentiable points too, which is why it is the safer test.
A zero of f' of even multiplicity never changes the sign of f'; a zero of odd multiplicity always does.

example.prompt: Classify the critical points of f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3.
example.work: f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2 = 4x^2(x - 3). The zeros are 0 (double) and 3 (simple). Sign: for x < 0, 4x^2 > 0 and x - 3 < 0, so f' < 0; for 0 < x < 3, again f' < 0; for x > 3, f' > 0. So f' falls then rises only at 3.
example.answer: Local minimum at x = 3 with f(3) = 81 - 108 = -27. x = 0 is stationary but not an extremum, because the sign of f' does not change there.

gateAngle: This is the test that rescues the cases where the second derivative vanishes. GATE CSE 2008 Q.25 is exactly such a case: at x = 2 the second derivative is 0, and the accepted solution falls back on the sign of f'(1) and f'(3), both positive, to conclude that x = 2 is not an extremum.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2008 Q.25: how many distinct extrema does 3x^4 - 16x^3 + 24x^2 + 37 have?
variations.answer: One. f'(x) = 12x(x - 2)^2 has zeros 0 and 2; the sign changes at 0 and not at 2.
variations.why: The sign chart, not the derivative's zeros, decides the count. Two critical points, one extremum.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Classify the critical points of f(x) = x^3(x - 2).
variations.answer: A local minimum at x = 3/2 and no extremum at x = 0. Here f = x^4 - 2x^3, so f'(x) = 4x^3 - 6x^2 = 2x^2(2x - 3); the critical points are 0 and 3/2, and the sign of f' changes only at 3/2, from negative to positive.
variations.why: A double root at 0 again, but now the surviving extremum is a minimum, which forces you to read the sign direction rather than pattern-match on the previous question.

trap.what: Counting every solution of f'(x) = 0 as an extremum.
trap.why: A repeated root of f' gives a stationary point where the function keeps increasing (or keeps decreasing), so no extremum exists there.
trap.counterexample: f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3 has f'(0) = 0 with f'(x) < 0 on both sides of 0, so 0 is not an extremum. GATE CSE 2008 Q.25 is the same phenomenon at x = 2.

check.question: f'(x) = (x - 1)^3 (x + 2). What happens at x = 1 and at x = -2?
check.answer: A local minimum at x = 1; a local maximum at x = -2.
check.explanation: The factor (x - 1)^3 is negative just left of 1 and positive just right, and (x + 2) is positive near 1, so f' goes from negative to positive: a minimum. At -2 the factor (x + 2) changes sign and (x - 1)^3 is negative there, so f' goes from positive to negative: a maximum.
